hypothesis: Three consecutive stability failures across three different reward-weight configurations make causal attribution impossible — every candidate culprit has been individually reverted, yet fell_over_rate remains ≈1.08–1.49 in the late window of each run. Critically, the original baseline configuration has never been directly tested. This experiment runs all parameters at manifest original values (reverting the air_time_reward_weight=0.4 deviation from Experiment 3 back to 0.2) to establish the first controlled anchor point. Two outcomes are possible: (1) baseline passes the stability gate (fell_over < 0.5 by ~iteration 1000), confirming air_time=0.4 or some prior change was the destabiliser and giving us a clean foundation for incremental gait-quality improvements; (2) baseline also fails, which would indicate structural instability in the task configuration (curriculum schedule, reset conditions, command velocity profile) that no reward weight can fix — shifting the investigation to curriculum parameters. Either outcome breaks the interpretability deadlock.
expected_effects: fell_over_rate drops below 0.5 by iteration ~1000 and stays there through the full run — this is the primary success criterion and establishes whether the baseline is stable

gait_contact_cv_mean stabilises near ~0.33–0.40 (the value seen at the start of each prior run before it degraded), rather than continuing the monotonic rise to 0.59+ seen in all three previous experiments
gait_air_cv_mean remains below 0.3 (swing regularity was acceptable in prior runs and should not regress)
track_linear_velocity reward remains near ~1.18–1.25 (no reward-competition pressure from the reverted changes)

If baseline also fails the stability gate (fell_over > 0.5 past iteration 1000), this is diagnostic: the instability is structural, not caused by any of the reward weight changes tested so far, and the next investigation must target curriculum velocity schedule or reset configuration
